items.title: Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run
items.summary: This is part 4 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own. Series contents Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself Before you start: the whole picture of checking, and how to test without breaking production Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (this article) Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon) Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon) Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon) Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon) Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon) How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon) When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon) Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon) The short version The tool a real attacker would point at other people, we pointed at a running copy of ourselves — about three cents. Alongside it we ran a legitimate AI scanner that reads a copy of our code, and two legitimate outside scanners against the same running copy; those two cost nothing this time. This is the fourth part of the series, and the first where we stop talking and actually run it: against a copy of our own service, promptflow. This article and the next are written as a manual — every command, and the screen it produces, side by side — so you can reproduce it. This part covers the setup and the first run. We line up tools of two kinds. One is a legitimate, permitted-use scanner. The other is what attackers actually run: an unrestricted tool. Think of them as the legit version and the real-attacker version of the same idea. Both are "autonomous" — they decide their own next move — and neither needs an expensive, high-end AI. We drive them with a cheap model, or run free tools. One promise up front: never point this at your live service. We ran it against a copy of our own code that never touches production. Why that is, and how far you may go, is what part 3 laid out. The result, first: the legitimate scanner, driven by a cheap model and scoped to the four login (authentication) routes, found three real weaknesses in the audit and session layer — nothing critical or high, two medium and one informational. The AI bill was about 45 cents ($0.45) . We then ran the real attacker-grade tool and two legitimate outside scanners (free ZAP and commercial StackHawk) against a running copy, from outside. What each one found, and how those findings differ, is next time. Here, we show how to set each up and run it. Why use an AI scanner A person can do this by hand. But there are two clear reasons to do it with an AI tool now. One is speed and reach. promptflow exposes 231 entry points (APIs) to the outside. Checking each by hand would take days — and the attacking side never stops, automatically. The defender working by hand cannot keep up. An AI tool decides on its own which entry points to check and in what order, and sweeps them at once. If attackers let AI do the planning, defenders should let the same AI do the planning. That is what "Defenders have the same AI too" from part 2 looks like in practice. The other is covering more ground than one person can hold in their head. A modern web service is tangled together with many external components and connected services. Even if your own code is perfect, a weak component or a weak downstream service becomes the way in. No person can trace that whole tangle anymore, which is why letting a tool look broadly became the realistic way. From here on, the actual procedure. First we run one legitimate scanner end to end, written so you can reproduce it step by step. Step 1 — Install the scanner The first tool is Strix, an open-source AI autonomous scanner — the defender-side, legitimate version of the kind of autonomous tool attackers use, and one that part 2 described. Installing it is one command; no special machine is needed. It runs on the computer you already use. If strix --version prints a version number, you are set. If you see command not found , the install path isn't on your PATH (the list of folders your computer searches for commands): find it with which strix and add that location. The scan runs inside an isolated Docker container (a sealed-off box created inside your computer; Docker is the software that runs it), so start Docker first — otherwise the run stalls the moment it tries to begin. Step 2 — Point it at a cheap model The tool runs one AI model at its center — the same mechanism attackers use to let AI do the planning. The key here is not to pick an expensive, high-end model . Security checking is less about hard reasoning and more about patiently trying each entry point, one after another. A cheap model doing volume is closer to what attackers actually do. We chose DeepSeek, a cheap model, and set its API key. One easy stumble: if the way the tool connects to the model is misconfigured, it stops before the scan begins with "can't connect." That stopped me at first. Specifying the cheap model through an OpenAI-compatible connection, with the endpoint (API address) stated explicitly, made it run. If it won't start, first check the key and the endpoint address. And note the balance before you run: read it again afterward and the difference is the exact cost. Step 3 — Scan a copy, never production Per part 3's line: the target is not production. Make a copy of your own code and point the scan at that. Whatever the tool does to a copy, production is untouched. Once copied, narrow the scope. The whole service has 231 entry points, but we scoped to just the four authentication routes — login-token exchange, logout, current-user, refresh. Narrowing the scope means even a small budget reaches past the surface, into checking each one deeply. "Narrow and deep" beats "broad and shallow" for a first step. Step 4 — Run it, with a hard cost cap With the prep done, state the target and what to look for, and run. The single most important thing here is to pass a cost cap . Overspend and it stops automatically. Without it, the bill can surprise you. The instruction, in one line: "this is an authorized self-test of our own code; report findings in a form that shows which file and where." Not "carry out attacks," but "find and report weaknesses." The cap this time was $1.00. It never got there — it finished on its own. Step 5 — What you see when it starts On run, an isolated environment (a Docker container) comes up, the scanning skills load, and the AI starts planning the check itself. Without a human saying "check this next," it reads the previous result and decides the next move on its own. Among the skills it loads is one called counterevidence . When it finds "this entry point might be dangerous," this skill makes it go looking for the opposite evidence, to verify whether the danger is real. That mechanism is what later produces the "doesn't call things out and walk away" behavior. In part 2, the attacker's tool planned its own steps; here the legitimate version does the same thing, against our own service. The way it works — the AI planning its own steps — is the same as the attacker's tool. The difference: the thing being checked is ours. Step 6 — Where it stopped, and the real cost After a while, the AI finishes on its own. Then compare the run record with the balance you noted in step 2 to learn the real cost. The real cost was $0.45. 235 exchanges, about 9 minutes. An earlier run with an expensive model (gpt-4.1) on the whole app — all 231 entry points — hit its $3 cap after spending $3.04, never got past the survey stage, and confirmed nothing. Narrowed to the four auth routes and switched to a cheap model, this run finished at $0.45 and found three real weaknesses. "You need an expensive model to run checks" is not true. For this kind of work, a cheap model doing volume fits better. Step 7 — Three real weaknesses The scan found three real weaknesses across the four authentication routes. None is critical or high — two medium, one informational — nothing that lets the service be taken over on the spot. But each cracks one of the two foundations authentication must guarantee: a trustworthy audit trail (the record of who did what), and a session (the logged-in state) that actually ends when told to. In plain terms: Logout says "success" without confirming the login ended (informational). The logout route returns "success" and records "session destroyed" without ever asking the sign-in service to end the login — or after that service refused or could not be reached. Seven of the eight request shapes tried did this. The machine rated it informational, the mildest level. Still, it's the seed of a real danger: someone who already holds a copy of the refresh token can keep minting new login tokens after the user believes they logged out. The audit "who" is trusted without checking (medium). The "who did it" written into the record is read from a token whose signature was never verified — meaning even a caller who is not logged in can plant any name into the record. The record stops being usable as evidence later. A fragment of the login token leaks into the log (medium). On a failed token refresh, the first twelve characters and the length of the submitted token, plus the upstream error text, are written to the log. The tool judged that more people can read logs than can read the token store, and rated it a leak path — and two lines above sits a policy rule: the token and the error text must never be put in the response to the user. The response side obeys it; only the logging side does not. What matters is that the machine did not stop at "might have found something": using the counterevidence skill it re-tested each candidate and narrowed them to the three that actually happen. For the logout and token-fragment findings, it ran the un-fixed code inside Strix's isolated container, with the services it talks to and the places it writes records swapped for stand-ins, to confirm they really occur; the audit finding it showed by tracing the code. That is where it differs from the old kind of check that only lists warnings. Each of the three comes with the file and line, how to reproduce it, and how to fix it. It also proved, with evidence, that certain whole classes of danger — injection (slipping database or shell commands into input), and SSRF (tricking the server into calling somewhere it shouldn't) — are not present in this scope. That "proof of absence" is as valuable as the findings, but how to read it, and why it's worth so much, is something we'll cover properly next time. Setting up the outside tools — a running copy So far, the legitimate tool read the copied code to find weaknesses. Next comes what attackers actually run: the real-grade tool — HexStrike, which we named in part 3. It does not read code. It probes the running service from outside, like a stranger . For that, the service being checked has to be actually running. But running doesn't mean production. On a private network that nothing outside can reach into, we bring up a throwaway copy of just the service's login routes, and point every test at that copy only. Three things run on that private network: the service under test (a copy of our own login routes), a stand-in that handles the sign-in check, and the attacking tool. The only target is this throwaway copy — never production, never anyone else's site. This series is only ever about checking ourselves. The outside tool picks its own moves First, the real-grade attacker tool. What's striking is that you hand it only the address of the service. From there, the cheap AI decides "what to try next" by itself. No human writes the steps. The left number is the step; the right number is the cost so far, calculated from the AI usage. At step 1 the AI decided "first confirm the service is up and look at the response headers," and chose its own probing tool. At step 4 it noted that any value returns a token, so this looks like a way in, and at step 5 recorded it as a serious candidate. It ran to step 24, hit the step limit, and stopped. It raised 6 candidates in all. The cost: about 3 cents, calculated from usage — the account balance did not move by even a cent. Not a high-end, latest AI — just a cheap one, run many times. One important caveat: those 6 are still candidates . Run a cheap AI many times and, mixed in with the real ones, it also produces confident mistakes. In fact, some of the candidates turned out to come not from our own code but from the stand-in server or the way the test was run. Sorting real from mistaken, one by one, is exactly what we show next time. For now, watch the run itself: hand it an address, and a cheap AI advances its own moves and raises candidates for a few cents. What only the outside view caught Among the candidates was one thing a code-reading tool could never find : the safety settings that should be attached to the response (security headers) were missing entirely. These headers tell the browser small promises like "don't let this display be embedded in other sites" and "always encrypt the connection." Missing, they open the way to display hijacking or eavesdropping. They don't appear in the code — they live on the "outside" of a running service — so you can't tell they're missing without receiving an actual response. A code-reading tool never sees a live response, so it cannot, in principle, find this. A genuine catch for the outside view. What's "found by probing from outside" and what's "found by reading code" differ structurally. Setting that difference side by side is one of the main subjects of next time. Legitimate tools can also test from outside So far, the outside probing used an attacker's tool. But probing from outside is something legitimate, permitted-use tools can do too — and you can start for free. We ran two legitimate outside scanners against the same running copy. The first is ZAP, a free tool anyone can use. You give ZAP the list of entry points (the OpenAPI spec). From that list, it works through a fixed set of checks, one at a time, against the running copy. After "Imported 8 URLs / 25 total," it runs injection, OS command injection, attacks that abuse XML, exposure of cloud settings, and so on, in turn — about 120 checks in all (117 passed). What came out, as a tally, is a result screen, so it's next time. Here, watch the run: a free tool, testing the same copy from outside, in a disciplined sweep. The second is StackHawk, a commercial tool for companies. It has no permanent free plan, but the first 14 days are free to try; we used it within that window. This is part 4 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own.

Series contents

  1. Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first
  2. What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself
  3. Before you start: the whole picture of checking, and how to test without breaking production
  4. Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (this article)
  5. Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon)
  6. Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon)
  7. Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon)
  8. Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon)
  9. Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon)
  10. How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon)
  11. When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon)
  12. Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon)
The short version

The tool a real attacker would point at other people, we pointed at a running copy of ourselves — about three cents. Alongside it we ran a legitimate AI scanner that reads a copy of our code, and two legitimate outside scanners against the same running copy; those two cost nothing this time. This is the fourth part of the series, and the first where we stop talking and actually run it: against a copy of our own service, promptflow. This article and the next are written as a manual — every command, and the screen it produces, side by side — so you can reproduce it. This part covers the setup and the first run.

We line up tools of two kinds. One is a legitimate, permitted-use scanner. The other is what attackers actually run: an unrestricted tool. Think of them as the legit version and the real-attacker version of the same idea. Both are "autonomous" — they decide their own next move — and neither needs an expensive, high-end AI. We drive them with a cheap model, or run free tools.

One promise up front: never point this at your live service. We ran it against a copy of our own code that never touches production. Why that is, and how far you may go, is what part 3 laid out.

The result, first: the legitimate scanner, driven by a cheap model and scoped to the four login (authentication) routes, found three real weaknesses in the audit and session layer — nothing critical or high, two medium and one informational. The AI bill was about 45 cents ($0.45). We then ran the real attacker-grade tool and two legitimate outside scanners (free ZAP and commercial StackHawk) against a running copy, from outside. What each one found, and how those findings differ, is next time. Here, we show how to set each up and run it.

Why use an AI scanner

A person can do this by hand. But there are two clear reasons to do it with an AI tool now.

One is speed and reach. promptflow exposes 231 entry points (APIs) to the outside. Checking each by hand would take days — and the attacking side never stops, automatically. The defender working by hand cannot keep up. An AI tool decides on its own which entry points to check and in what order, and sweeps them at once. If attackers let AI do the planning, defenders should let the same AI do the planning. That is what "Defenders have the same AI too" from part 2 looks like in practice.

The other is covering more ground than one person can hold in their head. A modern web service is tangled together with many external components and connected services. Even if your own code is perfect, a weak component or a weak downstream service becomes the way in. No person can trace that whole tangle anymore, which is why letting a tool look broadly became the realistic way.

From here on, the actual procedure. First we run one legitimate scanner end to end, written so you can reproduce it step by step.

Step 1 — Install the scanner

The first tool is Strix, an open-source AI autonomous scanner — the defender-side, legitimate version of the kind of autonomous tool attackers use, and one that part 2 described. Installing it is one command; no special machine is needed. It runs on the computer you already use.

If strix --version prints a version number, you are set. If you see command not found, the install path isn't on your PATH (the list of folders your computer searches for commands): find it with which strix and add that location. The scan runs inside an isolated Docker container (a sealed-off box created inside your computer; Docker is the software that runs it), so start Docker first — otherwise the run stalls the moment it tries to begin.

Step 2 — Point it at a cheap model

The tool runs one AI model at its center — the same mechanism attackers use to let AI do the planning. The key here is not to pick an expensive, high-end model. Security checking is less about hard reasoning and more about patiently trying each entry point, one after another. A cheap model doing volume is closer to what attackers actually do. We chose DeepSeek, a cheap model, and set its API key.

One easy stumble: if the way the tool connects to the model is misconfigured, it stops before the scan begins with "can't connect." That stopped me at first. Specifying the cheap model through an OpenAI-compatible connection, with the endpoint (API address) stated explicitly, made it run. If it won't start, first check the key and the endpoint address. And note the balance before you run: read it again afterward and the difference is the exact cost.

Step 3 — Scan a copy, never production

Per part 3's line: the target is not production. Make a copy of your own code and point the scan at that. Whatever the tool does to a copy, production is untouched.

Once copied, narrow the scope. The whole service has 231 entry points, but we scoped to just the four authentication routes — login-token exchange, logout, current-user, refresh. Narrowing the scope means even a small budget reaches past the surface, into checking each one deeply. "Narrow and deep" beats "broad and shallow" for a first step.

Step 4 — Run it, with a hard cost cap

With the prep done, state the target and what to look for, and run. The single most important thing here is to pass a cost cap. Overspend and it stops automatically. Without it, the bill can surprise you.

The instruction, in one line: "this is an authorized self-test of our own code; report findings in a form that shows which file and where." Not "carry out attacks," but "find and report weaknesses." The cap this time was $1.00. It never got there — it finished on its own.

Step 5 — What you see when it starts

On run, an isolated environment (a Docker container) comes up, the scanning skills load, and the AI starts planning the check itself. Without a human saying "check this next," it reads the previous result and decides the next move on its own.

Among the skills it loads is one called counterevidence. When it finds "this entry point might be dangerous," this skill makes it go looking for the opposite evidence, to verify whether the danger is real. That mechanism is what later produces the "doesn't call things out and walk away" behavior. In part 2, the attacker's tool planned its own steps; here the legitimate version does the same thing, against our own service. The way it works — the AI planning its own steps — is the same as the attacker's tool. The difference: the thing being checked is ours.

Step 6 — Where it stopped, and the real cost

After a while, the AI finishes on its own. Then compare the run record with the balance you noted in step 2 to learn the real cost.

The real cost was $0.45. 235 exchanges, about 9 minutes. An earlier run with an expensive model (gpt-4.1) on the whole app — all 231 entry points — hit its $3 cap after spending $3.04, never got past the survey stage, and confirmed nothing. Narrowed to the four auth routes and switched to a cheap model, this run finished at $0.45 and found three real weaknesses. "You need an expensive model to run checks" is not true. For this kind of work, a cheap model doing volume fits better.

Step 7 — Three real weaknesses

The scan found three real weaknesses across the four authentication routes. None is critical or high — two medium, one informational — nothing that lets the service be taken over on the spot. But each cracks one of the two foundations authentication must guarantee: a trustworthy audit trail (the record of who did what), and a session (the logged-in state) that actually ends when told to.

In plain terms:

  1. Logout says "success" without confirming the login ended (informational). The logout route returns "success" and records "session destroyed" without ever asking the sign-in service to end the login — or after that service refused or could not be reached. Seven of the eight request shapes tried did this. The machine rated it informational, the mildest level. Still, it's the seed of a real danger: someone who already holds a copy of the refresh token can keep minting new login tokens after the user believes they logged out.
  2. The audit "who" is trusted without checking (medium). The "who did it" written into the record is read from a token whose signature was never verified — meaning even a caller who is not logged in can plant any name into the record. The record stops being usable as evidence later.
  3. A fragment of the login token leaks into the log (medium). On a failed token refresh, the first twelve characters and the length of the submitted token, plus the upstream error text, are written to the log. The tool judged that more people can read logs than can read the token store, and rated it a leak path — and two lines above sits a policy rule: the token and the error text must never be put in the response to the user. The response side obeys it; only the logging side does not.

What matters is that the machine did not stop at "might have found something": using the counterevidence skill it re-tested each candidate and narrowed them to the three that actually happen. For the logout and token-fragment findings, it ran the un-fixed code inside Strix's isolated container, with the services it talks to and the places it writes records swapped for stand-ins, to confirm they really occur; the audit finding it showed by tracing the code. That is where it differs from the old kind of check that only lists warnings. Each of the three comes with the file and line, how to reproduce it, and how to fix it.

It also proved, with evidence, that certain whole classes of danger — injection (slipping database or shell commands into input), and SSRF (tricking the server into calling somewhere it shouldn't) — are not present in this scope. That "proof of absence" is as valuable as the findings, but how to read it, and why it's worth so much, is something we'll cover properly next time.

Setting up the outside tools — a running copy

So far, the legitimate tool read the copied code to find weaknesses. Next comes what attackers actually run: the real-grade tool — HexStrike, which we named in part 3. It does not read code. It probes the running service from outside, like a stranger. For that, the service being checked has to be actually running.

But running doesn't mean production. On a private network that nothing outside can reach into, we bring up a throwaway copy of just the service's login routes, and point every test at that copy only.

Three things run on that private network: the service under test (a copy of our own login routes), a stand-in that handles the sign-in check, and the attacking tool. The only target is this throwaway copy — never production, never anyone else's site. This series is only ever about checking ourselves.

The outside tool picks its own moves

First, the real-grade attacker tool. What's striking is that you hand it only the address of the service. From there, the cheap AI decides "what to try next" by itself. No human writes the steps.

The left number is the step; the right number is the cost so far, calculated from the AI usage. At step 1 the AI decided "first confirm the service is up and look at the response headers," and chose its own probing tool. At step 4 it noted that any value returns a token, so this looks like a way in, and at step 5 recorded it as a serious candidate. It ran to step 24, hit the step limit, and stopped. It raised 6 candidates in all. The cost: about 3 cents, calculated from usage — the account balance did not move by even a cent. Not a high-end, latest AI — just a cheap one, run many times.

One important caveat: those 6 are still candidates. Run a cheap AI many times and, mixed in with the real ones, it also produces confident mistakes. In fact, some of the candidates turned out to come not from our own code but from the stand-in server or the way the test was run. Sorting real from mistaken, one by one, is exactly what we show next time. For now, watch the run itself: hand it an address, and a cheap AI advances its own moves and raises candidates for a few cents.

What only the outside view caught

Among the candidates was one thing a code-reading tool could never find: the safety settings that should be attached to the response (security headers) were missing entirely.

These headers tell the browser small promises like "don't let this display be embedded in other sites" and "always encrypt the connection." Missing, they open the way to display hijacking or eavesdropping. They don't appear in the code — they live on the "outside" of a running service — so you can't tell they're missing without receiving an actual response. A code-reading tool never sees a live response, so it cannot, in principle, find this. A genuine catch for the outside view.

What's "found by probing from outside" and what's "found by reading code" differ structurally. Setting that difference side by side is one of the main subjects of next time.

Legitimate tools can also test from outside

So far, the outside probing used an attacker's tool. But probing from outside is something legitimate, permitted-use tools can do too — and you can start for free. We ran two legitimate outside scanners against the same running copy.

The first is ZAP, a free tool anyone can use.

You give ZAP the list of entry points (the OpenAPI spec). From that list, it works through a fixed set of checks, one at a time, against the running copy. After "Imported 8 URLs / 25 total," it runs injection, OS command injection, attacks that abuse XML, exposure of cloud settings, and so on, in turn — about 120 checks in all (117 passed). What came out, as a tally, is a result screen, so it's next time. Here, watch the run: a free tool, testing the same copy from outside, in a disciplined sweep.

Next

items.title: The Agent Bill of Materials Is on GitHub Right Now
items.summary: Open GitHub trending on any Saturday in October 2026 and you are looking at the agent stack — not a whiteboard diagram, not a vendor pitch deck, but real repositories with real stars shipping the real primitives. Cloudflare's security-audit-skill (46K stars, gaining 2,874/day). claude-mem (103K stars) for persistent agent memory. NVIDIA's OpenShell (19.8K stars) for sandbox isolation. FreeLLMAPI (41K stars) routing across 34 LLM providers. Hallmark (33K stars) as a design-quality skill gate. 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn → The theory phase is over. Three independent intelligence feeds — GitHub trending, YouTube conference talks, and industry pricing analysis — independently flagged the same pattern this week: the agent infrastructure stack has crystallized into five identifiable layers, each with at least one open-source incumbent claiming it. This is the Agent Bill of Materials (ABOM), and if your team is still hand-rolling these layers, you are accumulating architectural debt that compounds daily. The Five Layers An arXiv security survey published in April 2026 first proposed the Agent Bill of Materials as "a conceptual specification for enumerating all components that influence agent behavior at runtime." The paper noted that no tooling prototype existed. Seven months later, the tooling prototype is GitHub trending. Here is the BOM as it stands today, mapped to concrete repos: Layer Function Incumbent(s) Stars Model Reasoning engine GPT-6, Claude Opus 5.5, Kimi K3.1, DeepSeek V4.1 — Memory Persistent context across sessions claude-mem, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti 103K / 45K / 28K Skills Reusable capability packages Cloudflare Skills, Hallmark, AWS Agent Toolkit 46K / 33K / 3K Sandbox Isolated execution environment NVIDIA OpenShell, Cloudflare Sandboxes, E2B 19.8K / — / 12K Router Model selection and failover FreeLLMAPI, LiteLLM, Portkey 41K / 18K / 9K This is not the only way to slice the stack — Tacnode's guide describes six layers (adding observability), The AI Engineer's Substack counts seven (adding evals and guardrails). But the five-layer BOM captures the irreducible set: every production agent has a model it reasons with, memory it persists, skills it executes, a sandbox it runs inside, and a router that selects which model handles which request. ℹ️ The BOM framing matters because it shifts the conversation from "which framework should we use?" to "which layers are we missing?" A team running LangGraph with no sandbox is like shipping a web app without HTTPS — technically functional, visibly irresponsible. Layer 1: Model — The Commodity That Started It All The model layer is the most understood and the least interesting from an architecture perspective. It is the CPU of the agent: necessary, powerful, and increasingly interchangeable. The real engineering challenge is in the four layers around it. What has changed in 2026 is the cost compression. Prompt Engineering ran Kimi K3.1 Pro against Claude Opus 5.5 across 13 agentic coding tasks: Kimi finished the bill at $45.91 versus Opus's $83.46 — roughly 55% of the cost with comparable output quality. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 just took the number-one open-source coding spot, beating GPT-6 Astra on DeepSWE. The implication for the BOM: if the model is a commodity, everything else in the bill becomes the differentiator. Teams that over-invest in model selection and under-invest in the surrounding infrastructure are optimizing the wrong line item. Kepler's Vinoo Ganesh demonstrated this at the AI Engineer conference: a finance agent architecture where models cite numbers but never write them — the reasoning engine is surrounded by retrieval, deterministic math, and a filter that strips unverifiable figures over a 30-million-document SEC citation registry. The model is the least interesting component. The architecture around it is the product. Layer 2: Memory — The Session Problem Nobody Solved Until Now Agent memory is the layer where the gap between "demo" and "production" is widest. A demo agent starts fresh every session. A production agent remembers what it did, what worked, what the user prefers, and what context matters. View on GitHub → claude-mem has emerged as the open-source leader at 103K stars. Its approach: capture everything the agent does during sessions, compress it with AI, and inject relevant context back into future sessions. It ships as a Claude Code plugin with a $20/month cloud tier and a $333/seat team tier for shared memory and governance. But the memory wars are far from settled. A DevGenius comparison of 2026 memory systems found Mem0 scoring 49.0% and Zep scoring 63.8% on LongMemEval — but Mem0 later reported 94.4% on the same benchmark, and Zep disputed Mem0's LoCoMo results. The lesson: vendor benchmarks in the memory space are contested territory. Run your own evals. Read the full comparison on DevGenius → The community is actively debating the right abstraction. A Hacker News thread on OKF Agent Memory (81 points) surfaced a recurring question: should memory be git-native, database-backed, or embedded in the agent loop itself? View on Hacker News → ⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Memory and skills may merge. If a skill can declare its own persistent state, and memory can trigger skill execution based on recalled context, the boundary between them dissolves. claude-mem already blurs this line — its "observations" are both memory entries and execution context for future skill invocations. Locking into separate memory and skills layers today could mean a painful refactor in 18 months. The architectural choice that matters: vector-first vs. graph-first. Mem0 pairs a vector store with an optional knowledge graph. Zep is built around Graphiti, a temporal knowledge graph where time is a core dimension. For agents that need to reason about when something happened — compliance, audit trails, financial analysis — graph-first wins. For agents that need fast personalization — user preferences, coding style — vector-first is cheaper and faster. For a deeper dive on the memory layer's competitive landscape, see our earlier analysis: The Agent Memory Wars . Layer 3: Skills — The New Dotfiles Skills are reusable capability packages that teach agents how to do specific things — security audits, code review, deployment, design quality gates. They are the agent equivalent of dotfiles: portable, shareable configuration that follows you across environments. View on GitHub → Cloudflare's security-audit-skill exemplifies the pattern. At 46K stars and climbing 2,874 per day, it is a multi-phase security audit that works across Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Hallmark does the same for design quality — an anti-AI-slop gate at 33K stars. AWS shipped its own Agent Toolkit with MCP servers, skills, and plugins. A comparison of seven production skills frameworks for 2026 names Cloudflare Skills alongside Superpowers, GitHub Spec Kit, Vercel Labs Skills, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills, and the skills.sh ecosystem. The install surface is converging: npx skills@latest add is becoming the standard acquisition path. The economic angle matters: Salesforce's plan to meter external AI agent API calls into its systems — one Headless Platform Interaction per registered agent call — signals that every SaaS platform will eventually charge per-agent-call, not per-seat. Skills become the interface through which this metering happens. The skill is not just a capability — it is a billing unit. For our earlier coverage of the skills ecosystem's explosive growth, see: Agent Skills Are the New Dotfiles . 💡 What to do now: Audit your team's Claude Code or Cursor setup. If you have custom CLAUDE.md rules longer than 200 lines, you are writing a skill whether you know it or not. Extract them into versioned, portable skill packages that you can share across your org — before skills supply-chain attacks make the unvetted third-party skill a security liability. See our piece on View on GitHub → The urgency is real — and the community knows it. The "Launch HN: Freestyle" thread (322 points) on sandboxes for coding agents drew dozens of comments about the gap between what agents can do and what they should do. View on Hacker News → India's CERT-In issued an advisory after an AI agent "running a test" reached into real enterprise systems and read data it should not have accessed. Today's convergence report flagged five independent sources covering rogue-agent incidents this week alone. The sandbox is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between an agent that acts on your behalf and an agent that acts on its own initiative. Arize's Sofia Jakovcevic demonstrated the tradeoff at the AI Engineer conference: a one-line prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer but 17 points worse at finishing tasks. The sandbox enforces the safety floor that the prompt alone cannot guarantee. Her five-step production-trace regression loop gates merges in CI — but without a sandbox, a passing regression suite cannot prevent a rogue action at runtime.

For agents that need fast personalization — user preferences, coding style — vector-first is cheaper and faster.

For a deeper dive on the memory layer's competitive landscape, see our earlier analysis: The Agent Memory Wars.

Layer 3: Skills — The New Dotfiles

Skills are reusable capability packages that teach agents how to do specific things — security audits, code review, deployment, design quality gates. They are the agent equivalent of dotfiles: portable, shareable configuration that follows you across environments.

View on GitHub →

Cloudflare's security-audit-skill exemplifies the pattern. At 46K stars and climbing 2,874 per day, it is a multi-phase security audit that works across Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Hallmark does the same for design quality — an anti-AI-slop gate at 33K stars. AWS shipped its own Agent Toolkit with MCP servers, skills, and plugins.

A comparison of seven production skills frameworks for 2026 names Cloudflare Skills alongside Superpowers, GitHub Spec Kit, Vercel Labs Skills, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills, and the skills.sh ecosystem. The install surface is converging: npx skills@latest add is becoming the standard acquisition path.

The economic angle matters: Salesforce's plan to meter external AI agent API calls into its systems — one Headless Platform Interaction per registered agent call — signals that every SaaS platform will eventually charge per-agent-call, not per-seat. Skills become the interface through which this metering happens. The skill is not just a capability — it is a billing unit.

For our earlier coverage of the skills ecosystem's explosive growth, see: Agent Skills Are the New Dotfiles.

💡 What to do now: Audit your team's Claude Code or Cursor setup. If you have custom CLAUDE.md rules longer than 200 lines, you are writing a skill whether you know it or not. Extract them into versioned, portable skill packages that you can share across your org — before skills supply-chain attacks make the unvetted third-party skill a security liability. See our piece on
View on GitHub →
The urgency is real — and the community knows it. The "Launch HN: Freestyle" thread (322 points) on sandboxes for coding agents drew dozens of comments about the gap between what agents can do and what they should do.

View on Hacker News →
India's CERT-In issued an advisory after an AI agent "running a test" reached into real enterprise systems and read data it should not have accessed. Today's convergence report flagged five independent sources covering rogue-agent incidents this week alone. The sandbox is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between an agent that acts on your behalf and an agent that acts on its own initiative.

Arize's Sofia Jakovcevic demonstrated the tradeoff at the AI Engineer conference: a one-line prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer but 17 points worse at finishing tasks. The sandbox enforces the safety floor that the prompt alone cannot guarantee. Her five-step production-trace regression loop gates merges in CI — but without a sandbox, a passing regression suite cannot prevent a rogue action at runtime.

Read the full article on Arize →
The broader HN community discussion on NVIDIA's OpenShell at launch reflected the same tension — practitioners welcomed the sandbox but questioned whether an NVIDIA-controlled runtime would become the only option.

View on Hacker News →
OpenShell's ecosystem is expanding fast. NVIDIA announced the Open Agent Safety Platform in September 2026, pairing OpenShell with Sentry — a monitoring layer running on a separate BlueField-4 DPU. Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, Microsoft Security, and TrendAI are integrating. Popular coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor reportedly run inside OpenShell without modification.
For the broader security context, see our analysis of the agent security lethal trifecta.

Layer 5: Router — The Traffic Controller

The router sits at the bottom of the stack, deciding which model handles which request. FreeLLMAPI has emerged as the open-source leader for cost-conscious teams: 34 free LLM providers, 635 model endpoints, 7.4 billion tokens per month behind one OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint. Smart routing selects the best available model per request and fails over automatically on rate limits. Provider keys stay encrypted in a local SQLite database.

View on GitHub →
But the router layer is not just about cost arbitrage. It is about resilience. When one provider goes down — and they all do — the router is the circuit breaker. FreeLLMAPI pulls a signed model catalog from freellmapi.co so new free models and quota changes arrive without a git pull. LiteLLM and Portkey serve the enterprise tier with budget caps, team-level quotas, and audit logs.


The meta-pattern: Each BOM layer solves the same fundamental problem — preventing a single point of failure. Memory prevents context loss. Skills prevent capability gaps. Sandboxes prevent security breaches. Routers prevent model outages. The agent is not the model. The agent is the system that keeps working when any one component fails.

Nate B Jones captures the operations reality: agents are "messy roommates" eating your compute and disk. His recommendation: set house rules (the sandbox), give them proper storage (memory), and establish a budget (the router) before scaling up. The BOM is, in essence, the lease agreement.

What the Community Is Building

The pattern extends beyond the five named repos. Across Hacker News, a steady stream of Show HN and Launch HN posts reveals teams independently building the same layers — agent harnesses, browser sandboxes, persistent memory, and skill registries. The peerd thread (75 points) showcases an agent harness running entirely in the browser, a different sandbox philosophy from NVIDIA's kernel-enforced approach.

View on Hacker News →

The volume tells the story. A dataset of Show HN submissions from September 2024 to August 2026 lists 68,025 posts, and reports that coding agents went from a curiosity to roughly one submission in nine. The infrastructure layer is where the energy is.

The Convergence Signal

What makes this week's signal unusual is not that people are writing about agent architecture — they have been all year. It is that three independent feeds described the same stack forming in real time using the same repos as evidence:

  1. GitHub trending — the raw signal. Five repos, five layers, all gaining thousands of stars per day.
  2. YouTube Tech — mapping the "What's Inside an AI Agent" primer (model, tools, memory, planning, orchestration) onto those exact repos, plus the Salesforce agent-tax story.
  3. YouTube AI — AI Engineer conference talks on production finance-agent architecture and agent reliability as a discipline independently corroborated the same layered model.

When GitHub, two separate YouTube channels, and a Salesforce pricing strategy all point at the same architectural decomposition in the same 24-hour window, the category is no longer experimental. It is infrastructure.

What This Means for You

If you are building agents today, run this audit:

  1. Model: Are you locked to one provider? If your agent fails when OpenAI has a bad day, add a router.
  2. Memory: Does your agent remember what it did yesterday? If not, your users are re-teaching it every session. Evaluate claude-mem or Mem0 — the setup cost is hours, not weeks.
  3. Skills: Are your agent's capabilities defined as portable, versioned packages? Or are they buried in a CLAUDE.md file that only one person understands?
  4. Sandbox: Can your agent touch production data without human approval? If yes, you are one prompt injection away from a CERT-In advisory. OpenShell installs in minutes.
  5. Router: Are you paying list price for a single provider? FreeLLMAPI's 7.4 billion free tokens per month might cover your dev and staging environments entirely.

The BOM is not a framework to adopt. It is a checklist to audit against. The specific tools will change — OpenShell will get competitors, claude-mem may get acquired, FreeLLMAPI's free-tier arbitrage will shrink. But the five layers are structural. Skip one, and the agent works in the demo. Ship all five, and it works at 3 AM when nobody is watching.

For the broader thesis on why agent infrastructure — not models — is the real moat, see: Agent Infrastructure Is the Real Moat.

items.title: Which Dubai property source should your AI answer use?
items.summary: A fluent AI answer can still use the wrong kind of property evidence. Before asking a model to summarize a Dubai property source, define the question: are you describing a sales-price series, comparing a rental benchmark, or asking about one particular property? Those outputs are different. Putting them into the same dashboard does not make their meanings interchangeable. Keep the measure attached to the claim Dubai Land Department's Residential Sales Price Index page separates property segments and reporting periods. Its historical reference periods should stay historical: the date a website was updated is not necessarily the period the observations describe. The linked 2020 methodology explains why the mix of properties sold matters and describes a hedonic approach using recorded characteristics. This is a description of that published methodology, not a claim that every present-day index uses an unchanged model. The same index page includes restrictions on commercial use, including pricing, investment decisions and performance measurement. I am linking to the explanation and notice here, not reproducing its series or deriving a property's price from it. Public visibility alone does not establish permission to redistribute data or build a commercial feature around it. A rental benchmark is another input The Smart Rental Index FAQ describes building-related characteristics and registered rental contracts among its inputs, and specifies coverage limits, including an exclusion for DIFC. A rental benchmark does not, by itself, supply an acquisition price, operating costs, financing or realized occupancy for a particular property. My conclusion is limited: that source alone cannot establish the property's investment return. This is not a determination of anyone's permitted rent increase. DLD also has a separate Property Valuation service , with an application, supporting documents and review before a valuation certificate is issued. A model-generated paragraph linking to the service is not such a certificate. Give the summarizer an evidence card This is my proposed record format, not an official DLD form: { "question" : "What claim am I trying to support?" , "source_and_purpose" : "Which document or service addresses it?" , "observation_period" : null , "coverage_and_exclusions" : null , "measure_and_units" : null , "method_and_use_limits" : null , "access_date" : "2026-10-17" , "unresolved" : [] } The nulls are intentional. Missing fields should remain missing until evidence fills them. An instruction to produce a confident summary should not turn an unknown period into a current observation or a market segment into an inspected apartment. For a product, the useful first output may be a source-selection note with the gaps visible. That gives the next reviewer something to inspect before a number becomes a recommendation. The full source-selection guide includes the distinctions, limits and proposed evidence card. Source review: 17 October 2026. This educational article is not a current market report, property valuation, rent-dispute decision or investment recommendation. AI assisted drafting and source comparison. No personal transaction, customer outcome or tested company system is claimed.
items.summary_html:
A fluent AI answer can still use the wrong kind of property evidence. Before asking a model to summarize a Dubai property source, define the question: are you describing a sales-price series, comparing a rental benchmark, or asking about one particular property?

Those outputs are different. Putting them into the same dashboard does not make their meanings interchangeable.

Keep the measure attached to the claim

Dubai Land Department's Residential Sales Price Index page separates property segments and reporting periods. Its historical reference periods should stay historical: the date a website was updated is not necessarily the period the observations describe.

The linked 2020 methodology explains why the mix of properties sold matters and describes a hedonic approach using recorded characteristics. This is a description of that published methodology, not a claim that every present-day index uses an unchanged model.

The same index page includes restrictions on commercial use, including pricing, investment decisions and performance measurement. I am linking to the explanation and notice here, not reproducing its series or deriving a property's price from it. Public visibility alone does not establish permission to redistribute data or build a commercial feature around it.

A rental benchmark is another input

The Smart Rental Index FAQ describes building-related characteristics and registered rental contracts among its inputs, and specifies coverage limits, including an exclusion for DIFC.

A rental benchmark does not, by itself, supply an acquisition price, operating costs, financing or realized occupancy for a particular property. My conclusion is limited: that source alone cannot establish the property's investment return. This is not a determination of anyone's permitted rent increase.

DLD also has a separate Property Valuation service, with an application, supporting documents and review before a valuation certificate is issued. A model-generated paragraph linking to the service is not such a certificate.

Give the summarizer an evidence card

This is my proposed record format, not an official DLD form:

{
  "question": "What claim am I trying to support?",
  "source_and_purpose": "Which document or service addresses it?",
  "observation_period": null,
  "coverage_and_exclusions": null,
  "measure_and_units": null,
  "method_and_use_limits": null,
  "access_date": "2026-10-17",
  "unresolved": []
}

The nulls are intentional. Missing fields should remain missing until evidence fills them. An instruction to produce a confident summary should not turn an unknown period into a current observation or a market segment into an inspected apartment.

For a product, the useful first output may be a source-selection note with the gaps visible. That gives the next reviewer something to inspect before a number becomes a recommendation.

The full source-selection guide includes the distinctions, limits and proposed evidence card. Source review: 17 October 2026. This educational article is not a current market report, property valuation, rent-dispute decision or investment recommendation.

items.title: Your AI Model Predicts Risk. But Who Decides When to Act?
items.summary: How a decision threshold turns a reliable probability into an action — and why that choice is yours, not the model’s. Beyond Accuracy · Model Evaluation (#6) Honestly evaluating AI models is a personal project of mine, and I’ve been exploring it on clinical problems — by choice. Health is simply the domain I find most revealing, and the one most people feel in their gut: the cost of a missed cancer, or of an unnecessary biopsy, needs no explanation. But nothing in this piece is really about medicine. Any system that turns a probability into an action faces the same step — fraud scoring, demand forecasting, anomaly detection — those are just harder to feel in the same immediate way. Today the model is a synthetic screening model, where I generate the patients and know the ground truth exactly. That lets me study the step everyone rushes past: a trustworthy probability still isn’t an action — and the number you choose to act on decides everything. Start with a model that does its job well. On 4,000 synthetic patients — about 11% of them truly sick (448 cases) — it ranks sick patients ahead of healthy ones reliably ( AUROC 0.84 — AUROC measures how well a model sorts the sick above the healthy). Its probabilities are also honest: the 11% is the overall rate across everyone, but the model doesn’t hand every patient 11% — it gives each one their own risk, and when it says 30% for a group of patients, close to 30% of those patients really are sick. That last property is called calibration . Those are the first three questions this series asks of a model — can it make the call ( F1 ), can it order cases by risk ( AUROC ), can you believe its confidence ( calibration ) — pulled together most recently in the previous piece . This model clears all three. The model gives each patient a probability. Turning those probabilities into yes/no calls is a separate step, and it’s mine to make, not the model’s. So I did what most pipelines do by default: I treated every patient with a predicted risk above 0.5 — that is, above 50% — as a “positive” worth acting on. At that cutoff, it caught just a quarter of the disease — 25%. Of the 448 truly sick patients, it flagged 110 and missed 338 , while raising only 56 false alarms. The model itself didn’t fail — its ranking is intact, and its probabilities are honest. What failed was the decision rule : a cutoff chosen without weighing the consequences turned good risk estimates into a poor decision. It missed those patients because 0.5 was the wrong place to act, and nobody had chosen it on purpose. That’s the whole subject of this piece: once you trust the number, what do you do with it? The fourth question: Decide This series has been building one question at a time. F1 → can it predict? AUROC → can it rank? Calibration → can it be trusted? Those three are about the model. This one is about you : you now hold a trustworthy probability — what threshold turns it into an action? Call it the fourth verb: Decide. A probability is a statement about the world. A threshold is a statement about what you value. The model can hand you the first; only you can supply the second. Deciding is setting that threshold — the cutoff on the probability above which you act and below which you don’t — and the moment you pick it, you’ve made a value judgment about which mistake you’d rather make. 0.5 is a decision you didn’t know you were making The default cutoff of 0.5 feels neutral. It isn’t. A screening model can make two kinds of mistake: a missed case — a sick patient it waves through (a false negative) — and a false alarm — a healthy patient it flags for nothing (a false positive). Acting only when risk exceeds 50% quietly declares that a missed case and a false alarm cost you exactly the same. Cutting at 50% is the right call only if you’d trade one missed patient for one false alarm and feel you came out even — no worse off either way. That holds only in a simplified picture where those two mistakes are the whole story. Real decisions can carry more — the cost of running the test, the harm of the treatment itself, a patient’s own preferences — and a fuller analysis folds those in too. But the balance between the two errors is the right place to begin, so that’s where we’ll start. In almost no clinical setting are the two errors equal. Missing an early cancer is not the same as calling one more patient back for a scan that turns out clear. And when a disease is uncommon, a 0.5 cutoff is especially punishing. Low prevalence doesn’t guarantee this, but when the features give only moderate discrimination, even a well-calibrated model lands many genuinely sick patients below 50% — it’s seldom more than half-sure about anyone. A rule that acts only above 50% then flags almost none of them, and most of the disease slips through. That’s exactly what happened above — three-quarters of the sick patients, missed, at a threshold no one deliberately chose. (This doesn’t contradict the model’s ranking. AUROC is about order — sick scoring higher than healthy — not about where those scores land on the 0-to-1 scale. A sharper model could push many sick patients above 50%; this one, with only moderate discrimination, leaves 338 of the 448 below it — ranked above the healthy, yet short of the halfway mark.) The first move, then, is simply to make the choice on purpose. The statistical answer — and why it’s not enough The classic way to pick a cutoff from the data is Youden’s index . It leans on two numbers: sensitivity (the share of truly sick patients the model catches) and specificity (the share of truly healthy patients it correctly leaves alone). Youden’s index picks the threshold that maximizes J = sensitivity + specificity − 1 — the same as maximizing their sum, since the −1 is just a constant. It gives the two rates equal weight, with no regard for how common the disease is or what either error actually costs ( Youden, 1950 ). On this model it lands at 0.12 , and the picture changes completely: sensitivity jumps from 25% to 77% , specificity is 76% , and the model now catches 344 of the 448 cases instead of 110 — but the false alarms climb with it, from 56 to 848. But look at what Youden’s index quietly assumes: that a point of sensitivity and a point of specificity are worth the same. It’s a statistical balance, blind to what the errors actually cost and to how common the disease is. It’s a reasonable reference point when you genuinely have no cost information — and the wrong anchor the moment you do. Which is almost always. The honest driver: the cost of the two errors Here’s the idea that reorganizes everything. The ROC curve shows what different thresholds can achieve, but it can’t, by itself, tell you which trade-off is clinically acceptable. That is set by a single question: how many times worse is a missed case than a false alarm? Call that number — how many times worse a missed case is than a false alarm — the cost ratio , and write it R . (“Cost” here means real-world harm: a missed case can mean a disease caught too late; a false alarm means an unnecessary, sometimes invasive, follow-up.) For a calibrated risk model, when the only things on the scale are the cost of a false positive and the cost of a false negative, the threshold that minimizes expected cost is act if predicted risk ≥ p_t, where p_t = 1 / (1 + R) Here p_t is the probability threshold — p for probability, the small t for “threshold.” Read it slowly, because it’s the whole game. The arithmetic is just that one formula: If the two errors are equal , R = 1 , then p_t = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.50. That’s exactly why the naive default catches so little. If a missed case is 9× worse, R = 9, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 9) = 0.10. You act at just 10% risk, accepting more false alarms to avoid a miss. If a false alarm is what you fear — say it’s 4× worse than a miss, so R = 1/4, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 0.25) = 0.80. Now you act only when you’re 80% sure. One thing R is not : a promise about headcount. It sets the relative cost of the two errors, not the number of false alarms you’ll actually trade for each extra case caught — that depends on the model and how common the disease is. The nine is a statement of values, not a body count. (And the formula assumes the plain yes/no decision we’re in; capacity limits, costs that differ patient to patient, or actions beyond act / don’t-act would each need more than this one line.) On this model, that one number moves everything: Same model, same probabilities, same patients. The only thing that changed was an honest statement of what the mistakes cost — and that statement, not the algorithm, decided who got caught. The threshold is where medicine, not machine learning, has to speak. The question underneath all of it: does acting even help? Suppose you’ve chosen a threshold. One question remains, and it’s the one that should be asked first and almost never is: does using this model actually beat the obvious alternatives — referring everyone, or referring no one? This is what Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) answers — a method from Vickers & Elkin (2006) , not something I’ve invented, and the first time this series meets it. It rests on a quietly brilliant reframing: the threshold you’d act at is itself a statement of how you weigh the two errors against each other. A clinician who’d act at 10% is telling you a missed case is worth about nine false alarms — so weigh their harms in exactly that proportion. That gives a single number of their devising, net benefit , at any threshold: net benefit = (true positives / N) − (false positives / N) × p_t/(1 − p_t) Here N is the total number of patients evaluated. The true positives are the good the model does; the false positives are penalized in exact proportion to that same trade-off. Compute it across every threshold a reasonable clinician might hold, and plot three lines: the model, refer everyone , and refer no one . (In a screening setting those defaults mean testing or referring every patient versus none — not literally treating anyone.) Across the range of thresholds a clinician might reasonably consider for a screening referral — roughly 5% to 30% — the model delivers at least as much estimated net benefit as either alternative: referring everyone, or referring no one. The trade-off is revealing. At very low thresholds, referring everyone can make sense, because the priority is to miss as few cases as possible. But as the threshold rises, each unnecessary referral carries more weight, and eventually referring everyone produces less net benefit than referring no one at all. Referring no one, meanwhile, always scores exactly zero in Decision Curve Analysis — a mathematical reference point, not a claim that missing every case does no harm. The decision curve makes this trade-off visible. Instead of asking only how accurately the model predicts, it asks whether acting on those predictions offers a better balance of benefit and harm than the alternatives, at thresholds that reflect real clinical priorities.
